chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ibrahim ibn Ishaq, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from his father, from his grandfather al-Hasan ibn Rashid, from Muhammad al-Attar, who said:

I traveled with Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) to Mecca, and he ordered his slave to do something, but the slave disobeyed and did something else. Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said, 'By Allah, I will surely strike you, O slave.' He said, and I did not see him strike him. So I said, 'May I be your ransom, you swore that you would strike your slave, yet I did not see you strike him.'
Is it not that Allah says, 'And to forgive is nearer to piety (taqwa)'?
ai.seo_question: Why did the Imam withhold punishment after swearing to strike his slave?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) demonstrates the principle of *kaffarah* (expiation) and the virtue of leniency by withholding the strike he swore to deliver, citing the Quranic ideal that forgiveness is closer to *taqwa*. This incident highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on balancing the sanctity of oaths with the higher ethical objective of mercy, showing that one should not rigidly enforce an oath if it leads to unnecessary harshness. The Imam’s action serves as a practical model for believers to prioritize spiritual consciousness over literal fulfillment of minor vows.
